en: Thinking all would be as a fire gone out,
Let mighty Kyyaz take
This head as his spoil,
She of silver eyes and sun-bright face,
The pillar of heroes among the brave,
The leader of the people among champions,
Wished that he might leave descendants behind.
Letting the goose be devoured by birds of prey,
Because of a single camel calf
She let herself be called a captive wife;
For this she had come as spoil,
Making the Kalmyk’s head a mountain,
And raising a woman’s head as a hero,
She had given her heart to Kyyaz.
The dear woman Aichürök,
When twilight fell and the sun went down,
When all the people lay fast asleep,
Would spread out the hair upon her back;
Into brave Kyyaz’s embrace—
Let us begin again from here:
The moon waned and the days passed,
And so many years went by.
When Kyyaz took Chürök that day,
When he laid waste to Talas,
Akun’s unfortunate daughter
Had intended to die,
But remained alive instead—
For the hero had left within her
A child of four months.
She meant to depart in her grief,
Yet remained alive and did not go;
Semetey had left within her
A child three months in the craving.
She meant to die from shame,
Yet your sister-in-law remained alive,
Because the ill-fated one in her womb
Was a token left by her beloved.
Parted from her hero,
The wretched, distraught Aichürök
Lamented and burned with grief.
Saying, “A token of the hero remains,”
This tormented, ill-fated woman
Made the three-month child in her womb
Her hope and consolation.
Sobbing and crying aloud,
She meant to die from shame,
Yet remained alive,
Because hope lay within her womb.
“My bloodthirsty lord is dead,” she said,
Mist rises from the ravine;
When misfortune is truly driven to fury,
It finds a thousand true devices.
She reads Arabic spells and blinds the eyes,
Turns into a white swan and alters the weather.
Do not call Chürök ordinary,
With all her wondrous powers;
Do not think Chürök insignificant,
So extraordinary is her nature.
The beauty of that unfortunate woman,
Her lovely form, was found in no mortal,
Nor was the precious grace of her heart.
By day she pleased Kyyaz,
Delighting and beguiling his soul;
When night fell, she deceived Kyyaz
By casting a spell upon his eyes.
Thus not the slightest suspicion
Remained in Kyyaz’s mind.
The renowned Aichürök
Stayed beside Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
Flirting with him
Throughout the day.
At night she blinded
The hero Kyyaz’s eyes
And deceived him.
She would lie with her back turned to him,
And every day, disguising
One of the attendants herself,
She would give Kyyaz
One of the young women beside her.
A rivered spring beneath a sheer cliff—
Will it yield its heart when it dies,
Such a wretched creature as that?
The days waned and the months passed;
Since brave Kyyaz had taken Chürök,
Nine months were completed,
And nearly ten months had passed.
Her womb grew ripe and her term was full,
The appointed time and day arrived.
Beside moonlike Chürök
Were her attendants,
Sixty young wives and eighty maidens;
Disguising them as herself,
She sent one each day
Into Khan Kyyaz’s embrace.
Keeping her chaste self pure,
Preserving herself untouched by anything,
Dear Aichürök
Protected herself in this way.
The unfortunate woman possessed sacred powers
And many miracles;
Among women in flowing gowns,
She was a soul who surpassed them all.
The tormented, ill-fated woman
Had a seal upon her tongue.
She could sweep along at a horse’s speed
And fly throughout
The whole wide world;
Such was the magic she possessed.
Only Friday knew of her flight,
Only the sacred night knew of her travels;
When she transformed and flew,
Who could know of that single flight?
She made the open plains her wondrous summer pasture,
Chanting incantations like a sorcerer
And casting blindness over human eyes.
Of all the wisdom granted humankind,
Not a hair’s breadth was lacking in her.
Her curse was dreadful, her venom strong;
Whomever she cursed, she laid low.
Those who saw her majesty trembled;
She knew with perfect mastery
The magic that blinded eyes.
When she transformed into a white swan,
Only the darkening night knew of her flight;
Who else could know that she had gone?
When she unleashed her powers fully,
She turned a summer day to winter
And froze every summer pasture.
When the distraught woman gathered her strength,
“Let this burning anguish subside,” she prayed,
Seeking a remedy from Allah,
The unfortunate woman beseeching God
For the child within her womb.
“Grant him to me,” she pleaded;
“What will he endure
Among bitter enemies?
If my appointed days end and death comes,
What will become of him when I die?
How shall I ever see
The renowned young gray wolf,
Born of my blood and dark eyes,
The brave boy I have longed for,
The hero destined before me?
Alas, countless worries have torn apart my mind
For the child sprung from my loins.
Without letting the enemy suspect,
Can I entrust him to someone’s care?
If they use force without warning,
If they suddenly commit violence,
Will they fear the watching eye?
Will they act as enemies
To the brave boy left by the lion?
Will they kill him without delay,
Before he reaches maturity?”
Countless cares would not fit within her breast,
Her tears streamed in a thousand rivulets;
The poor woman wept all the more.
The reason she wept
Was that she had been taken as spoil;
The unfortunate woman wept in sorrow
Because she had been given an evil name.
The reason she wept was this:
She had no strong protector,
No secure place to shelter,
No forest into which she could flee,
No Nogoy people to defend her;
Her misery was beyond measure.
She had no renowned Kyrgyz people,
Mighty as mountains, to be her hope.
Thus her labor came upon her.
On the sacred night of Friday,
During the day of Thursday,
Full labor came
Upon moonlike Chürök,
The wise and wondrous woman.
Her spirits failed and her flesh ached;
Labor came upon Chürök.
Blood came as the sign of the child;
Seeing the sign, she cried aloud,
And Aichürök’s strength deserted her.
Her back throbbed with terrible pain;
All her sixty joints and forty-one bones
Ached without a single exception.
Whenever Chürök sat down,
Both her dark thighs hurt;
The poor woman’s bladder also ached,
Leaving her unable to move.
Her whole body hurt,
Her most intimate parts were in pain;
Her labor became a terrible affliction.
She screamed and cried aloud,
Sobbing because she could not endure it.
Her ribs seemed to split apart
And tears poured from her eyes;
Cruel, accursed death
Seemed close before her eyes.
Sobbing, the woman Aichürök
Spent her frail, fly-like life,
Screaming and crying aloud:
“Show me the brave boy left by my khan,
The heir left by the bloodthirsty hero,
The banner fastened to the spear,
The gift bestowed by the betrothed,
The hoofprint left by the noble steed,
The brave boy left by the falcon—
O God, show him to me unharmed!
Make this grievous pain subside,
Brighten this mirror-like face!”
Her spirit was sorrow and her heart was pain;
This woman earnestly begged
The true God for a child.
After seven days had passed,
When Chürök’s true labor
Had lasted seven days,
Her blood was spent and her strength was gone,
Her power failed and her breath grew faint.
Wailing and wasting away for the child,
She was left utterly helpless.
Then Aichürök
Raised her voice in a scream;
The lifeless trees wept,
All the Creator’s works wept,
Every living creature wept—
Chürök’s ordeal had begun.
Sixty stars and seven wild sheep,
Arrayed high overhead,
The moon and stars sharing her travail,
Labored together above her.
Gathering all around,
The shamans of every tribe
Joined her travail in a great throng.
Then Aichürök
Labored without pause for eight days;
Only a spoonful of blood remained.
She lost consciousness, unable even to groan,
And her flesh became a bruised, blue pulp.
She had no voice left even to moan,
And no strength remained
To hide her state from Kyyaz of the Jediger.
Agonized by true labor,
The poor woman could endure no more
And despaired of her frail, fly-like life.
When nine days had passed,
There was no way to restrain herself;
None of her own gathered people were there.
When the bright dawn advanced
And its first light glimmered,
When daylight touched the earth,
Stars poured down from the sky.
Her many thoughts unraveled,
Her bewildered mind broke apart;
The dark earth, sealed below,
Seemed ready to take her
If her head survived this ordeal.
From the distraught poor woman’s
Quail-like eyes,
